## Motivation: Complex Variable Dependencies in Multivariate Time Series

Building predictive diagnostic models for multivariate time series often begins with feature selection. A standard machine learning reflex is to compute a linear correlation matrix to identify and drop redundant variables. While useful for simple stochastic processes, this linear assumption frequently breaks down in physical domains.

In industrial IoT, for example, variables are governed by causal, closed-loop mechanics. To illustrate this, we load the `hvac_features` dataset (Turin HVAC telemetry [@borda2022development]) provided with `isoRouting` and examine the linear correlation across its 11 telemetry channels.


```{r}
#| label: load-data
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Show Data Loading"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(isoRouting)

# Load the bundled package data
data("hvac_features", package = "isoRouting")

# Restrict to the raw variables (the package data also contains engineered features)
hvac_raw <- hvac_features |> 
  select(
    t_supply, t_return, sp_return, t_saturation, t_outdoor, 
    rh_supply, rh_return, rh_outdoor, energy, power
  )

```

```{r}
#| label: fig-correlation
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8
#| code-summary: "Show EDA Code"
#| fig-cap: "Global Pearson correlation heatmap (Turin HVAC Raw Telemetry)"

library(ggcorrplot)

# Calculate correlation matrix
cor_matrix <- cor(hvac_raw, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

# Set the diagonal to NA to de-emphasize trivial self-correlations
diag(cor_matrix) <- NA

# Generate the square ggplot-based heatmap
ggcorrplot(
  cor_matrix,
  method = "square",
  type = "full",
  lab = TRUE,              
  lab_size = 3.5,
  lab_col = "black",       
  colors = c("#f8766d", "white", "#00bfc4"), 
  outline.color = "gray90",
  legend.title = "Correlation"
) +
theme(
  axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust = 1, face = "bold"),
  axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold")
) +
scale_y_discrete(limits = rev)
```

Based on the heatmap one could be tempted to remove some variables with high correlation and ignore low correlation coefficients. However, examining the raw pairwise dependencies reveals a much more complex geometric reality.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pairs-plot
#| eval: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Show EDA Code"
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 12
#| fig-cap: "Scatterplot matrix with correlation-mapped backgrounds (Sampled at n=5000)"

library(GGally)

# 1. Custom function to calculate correlation and map it to a background color
custom_scatter_bg <- function(data, mapping, ...) {
  x_data <- GGally::eval_data_col(data, mapping$x)
  y_data <- GGally::eval_data_col(data, mapping$y)
  
  corr <- cor(x_data, y_data, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
  
  color_fun <- colorRamp(c("#f8766d", "white", "#00bfc4")) 
  scaled_corr <- (corr + 1) / 2 
  
  rgb_vec <- color_fun(scaled_corr)
  hex_color <- rgb(rgb_vec[1], rgb_vec[2], rgb_vec[3], maxColorValue = 255)
  
  ggplot(data, mapping) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, 
             fill = hex_color, alpha = 0.4) +
    geom_point(...)
}

# 2. Generate the plot for a representative sample using the restricted raw data
set.seed(42)
p_pairs <- hvac_raw |>
  sample_n(5000) |> 
  ggpairs(
    lower = list(continuous = wrap(custom_scatter_bg, alpha = 0.1, size = 0.5)),
    upper = list(continuous = wrap(custom_scatter_bg, alpha = 0.1, size = 0.5)),
    title = "Pairwise Scatterplot Matrix (HVAC Raw Telemetry)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "gray80", fill = NA)
  )

p_pairs
```

The scatterplot matrix shows that linear correlation is an inadequate measure here. Variables form distinct geometric manifolds, dense operational clusters, and hard boundaries dictated by mechanical limits and programmed setpoints.   

Explicitly modeling these dependencies using traditional parametric methods would require a prohibitive expansion of polynomial and interaction terms. 

This geometric complexity is why `isoRouting` utilizes the Isolation Forest algorithm [@liu2008isolation]. Rather than attempting to explicitly model the dense, intricate topology of "normal" operations, the Isolation Forest uses non-Euclidean random partitioning to efficiently isolate anomalies that fall outside these manifolds.

To make anomaly detection actionable in an operations research context, isoRouting establishes a two-tiered diagnostic framework that decouples system explanation from operational alerting:

- **Archetype Discovery (Explaining Faults)**: By capturing a broader statistical substrate of anomalous time courses, the engine provides sufficient data density to map distinct operational manifolds. Clustering this substrate yields spatial medoids—the representative profiles of underlying deviations from nominal variable interactions. Rather than classifying every point in this subset as a critical failure, these profiles are used to map the distinct operating regions associated with anomalous behavior.
- **Threshold Triggers (Alerting on Severity)**: Once the underlying behavioral departures are established, a higher anomaly score threshold is applied to govern active alerts. By restricting real-time alarms to the most extreme scores (a fraction of a percent of total observations), the system prevents operator fatigue. When an extreme alert fires, its proximity to a pre-computed medoid immediately associates it with a known fault archetype, enabling rapid root-cause diagnosis or flagging a novel anomaly type.


## Data Preparation and Temporal Integrity

The first step in the `isoRouting` pipeline is preparing the raw time-course data. Because the engine's core methods rely on interpretable time intervals, DiagnosticEngine strictly requires a properly formatted datetime column named timestamp (POSIXt).

We begin by loading the Turin HVAC dataset bundled with the package and verifying our time column:

```{r}
#| label: data-ingestion
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Show Data Loading"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(isoRouting)
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)

# Load the package-associated Turin HVAC dataset
data("hvac_features", package = "isoRouting")

# Verify the timestamp column is present and properly classed
class(hvac_features$timestamp)
```

Before initializing the engine, we must ensure there are no missing epochs that could skew the dynamical windowing. We use the `check_time_continuity()` helper to scan the dataset:

```{r}
#| label: continuity-check
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Show Continuity Check"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Evaluate temporal continuity
continuity_check <- check_time_continuity(hvac_features$timestamp)

# Flag returns FALSE if gaps are detected
print(continuity_check)
```

The output of `check_time_continuity()` provides a boolean flag alongside a summary of all time intervals between consecutive rows. While the expected polling interval for the Turin HVAC system is 900 seconds (15 minutes), the `$summary` component exposes a large discontinuity of 15,814,800 seconds (approximately 6 months), alongside several smaller outages ranging from a few hours to six days.

Ingesting a 6-month gap would severely distort estimations performed by `isoRouting`. However, the underlying Isolation Forest and distance matrices can handle minor maintenance downtimes without requiring synthetic data imputation.

Therefore, we will split the dataset into two distinct operational periods across the 6-month boundary. We will use both early and late segments for different purposes in this vignette.

```{r}
#| label: data-split-and-validation
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Show Data Split"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Calculate time differences to locate the massive 6-month gap
time_diffs <- as.numeric(difftime(
  hvac_features$timestamp[-1], 
  hvac_features$timestamp[-nrow(hvac_features)], 
  units = "secs"
))

# Dynamically find the index of the absolute largest gap (the 6-month shutdown)
major_gap_idx <- which.max(time_diffs)

# Bucket 1: Pre-Gap, ~40% of data
baseline_telemetry <- hvac_features |> 
  slice(1:major_gap_idx)

# Bucket 2: Post-Gap, ~60% of data
stream_telemetry <- hvac_features |> 
  slice((major_gap_idx + 1):n())

# Validate bucket 1: 
# We set tolerance to 7 days (604800 seconds) to allow for 1- to 6-day maintenance 
baseline_check <- check_time_continuity(baseline_telemetry$timestamp, tolerance = 604800)

if (!baseline_check$is_continuous) {
  stop("Bucket 1 contains structural time discontinuities.")
} else {
  cat("Bucket 1 temporal integrity verified. Minor outages are within 7-day tolerance.\n")
}

# Validate bucket 2: 
stream_check <- check_time_continuity(stream_telemetry$timestamp, tolerance = 604800)

if (!stream_check$is_continuous) {
  stop("Bucket 2 data contains structural time discontinuities.")
} else {
  cat("Bucket 2 temporal integrity verified. Minor outages are within 7-day tolerance.\n")
}
```

## Engine Configuration and Initialization

The `DiagnosticEngine` relies on a YAML configuration file to define its machine learning hyperparameters and feature schema (variables to use). To begin, we configure the engine using a "naive" approach, passing the raw physical sensor readings directly into the model.

In `isoRouting`, the feature schema partitions variables into two types:

- **Target Variables:** The feature space the Isolation Forest uses to score anomalies and the engine uses to compute topological distances.
- **Context Variables:** Variables excluded from the mathematical model, but retained within the extracted medoid windows to provide human-interpretable context during visual analysis.

In our naive configuration, we assign all primary temperature, humidity, and power metrics as target variables, leaving the context variables empty. We instantiate the S4 object by calling `new("DiagnosticEngine", config_path = ...)`, pointing it to our YAML file.

```{r}
#| label: naive-initialization
#| warning: false
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Show Naive Configuration and Instantiation"

# Define the naive YAML schema using raw sensor values
yaml_naive <- "
ntrees: 500
sample_size: 256
temporal_window_hours: 2
anomaly_threshold: 0.60
context_variables: []
target_variables:
  - t_supply
  - t_return
  - sp_return
  - t_saturation
  - t_outdoor
  - rh_supply
  - rh_return
  - rh_outdoor
  - energy
  - power
"

# Write the configuration to a temporary file for ingestion
config_naive <- tempfile(pattern = "naive_config_", fileext = ".yml")
writeLines(yaml_naive, config_naive)

# Instantiate the DiagnosticEngine
engine <- new("DiagnosticEngine", config_path = config_naive)

# Verify the target and context variables parsed from the schema
get_features(engine)
```

## Time Course Ingestion

Once the engine is configured, the next step is to load the dataset into the S4 object using the `ingest_time_course()` method.

This method performs validation checks before locking the data into the engine. It verifies that the required `timestamp` column is present and properly formatted, and it ensures that variables listed under `target_variables` in the YAML schema exist within the provided dataframe. 

Crucially, the engine strictly enforces the schema: it culls any extraneous columns not defined as target or context variables, caching only the authorized dataset for memory-efficient downstream anomaly extraction.

```{r}
#| label: ingest-time-course
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Show Data Ingestion"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Ingest the historical baseline telemetry into the engine
engine <- ingest_time_course(engine, data = baseline_telemetry)

# Verify the updated lifecycle state of the engine
engine@domain_state

# Inspect the ingested data structure (note: features not included in the yaml are dropped)
glimpse(get_time_course(engine))
```

## Anomaly Extraction via Isolation Forest

With the time course ingested and cached in the engine, we now trigger the anomaly extraction phase using `extract_anomalies()`. 

The `DiagnosticEngine` employs an Isolation Forest (`isotree`) to score the feature space. Unlike distance-based algorithms, Isolation Forests isolate anomalies by randomly selecting a feature and a split value. Anomalies—being "few and different"—require fewer splits to be isolated, resulting in shorter path lengths in the forest's decision trees.

The engine uses the hyperparameters defined in our YAML schema (e.g., `ntrees: 500`, `sample_size: 256`) to build the forest. It then scores every observation in our baseline telemetry. Any event with an empirical anomaly score exceeding our YAML-defined threshold (`0.60`) is permanently isolated for downstream topological routing.

```{r}
#| label: extract-anomalies
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Show Anomaly Extraction"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Score the feature space and extract extreme events
engine <- extract_anomalies(engine)

# Verify the engine state
engine@domain_state

# The isolated events are now cached in the anomalies slot. 
# We can check how many extreme events exceeded our threshold:
nrow(engine@anomalies)
```


## Visualizing the Threshold Landscape

Before extracting anomalies, `isoRouting` has two methods that are helpful to explore the  relationship between anomaly score threshold $\theta$ and number $N$ of points with score above $\theta$.

Method `explore_thresholds()` rapidly scores the feature space without mutating the engine's internal state. This allows users to visualize the decay curve of extreme events.

```{r}
#| label: naive-explore-thresholds
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Show Threshold Exploration"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Generate a threshold landscape for the ingested baseline telemetry
threshold_curve <- explore_thresholds(engine, thresholds = seq(0.50, 0.75, by = 0.01))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-naive-threshold-decay
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Show Visualization Code"
#| fig-cap: "Anomaly threshold decay curve showing the reduction in isolated extreme events as the Isolation Forest score threshold increases."
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(ggplot2)

# Plot the decay of extreme events
ggplot(threshold_curve, aes(x = Threshold, y = Event_Count)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "darkblue", size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.60, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Anomaly Threshold Decay Curve",
    subtitle = "Red dashed line indicates the 0.60 YAML selection",
    x = "Isolation Forest Threshold",
    y = "Number of Extracted Events"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Conversely, method `get_threshold_at_N()` enables the user to find the value of $\theta$ that yields at least $N$ anomalies.

```{r}
#| label: get-threshold_at_N
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Show get_threshold_at_N Call"

threshold <- get_threshold_at_N(engine, 40)
cat(paste0("Threshold = ", signif(threshold, digits = 3), " yields at least 40 anomalies"))
```

These two basic methods are complemented with a more complex one presented next.

## Threshold Diagnostics

```{r}
#| label: naive-evaluate-stability
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Show evaluate_k_stability Call"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Sweep based on statistical substrate size (N)
stability_curve_naive <- evaluate_k_stability(engine, max_N = 800, min_N = 20, nb_steps = 61, max_k = 10)

```

Method `evaluate_k_stability()` maps the anomaly threshold against three independent diagnostics:

- **Optimal Clusters ($k$)**: At each value of threshold $\theta$, divisive clustering [@kaufman1990finding] is utilized to group anomalies. Rather than relying on Euclidean space or native, sample-size-dependent isolation-forest distances, the engine extracts the terminal node matrix from the isolation forest (`isotree`). It then computes the proportional Hamming distance—the fraction of trees in the forest where two observations land in different terminal leaves. Because this metric measures structural disagreement, it is independent of the dataset size. The optimal number $k$ of clusters (best tree cut) is then defined as the one maximizing the global silhouette score [@rousseeuw1987silhouettes]. Visualization of $k$ as a function of $\theta$ helps identify $\theta$ intervals where clustering is stable.
- **Hartigan's Dip Statistic ($D$)**: The statistic (effect size) of a non-parametric test applied to the Hamming distance matrix. A peak in $D$ rejects the hypothesis of unimodality, indicating maximum distance heterogeneity (i.e., the likely presence of highly distinct clusters) [@hartigan1985dip].
- **Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID)**: Measures how many variables remain independent. A decrease in LID suggests a system "breakdown," where variables become more coupled due to a physical fault (e.g. a sensor break will decrease variance of a variable).

<b id="stability-ggplot-target" class="flash-target">Diagnostics Plotting Wrapper</b>
```{r}
#| label: stability-ggplot-function
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Show ggplot Function"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# Define a reusable plotting wrapper
plot_topological_stability <- function(stability_df, plot_title, plot_subtitle) {
  
  # Pivot the profile dataframe for multi-panel plotting
  plot_data <- stability_df |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = c(N_Anomalies, Opt_k, Hartigans_D, Global_LID), 
      names_to = "Metric", 
      values_to = "Value"
    ) |>
    mutate(Metric = factor(Metric, levels = c("N_Anomalies", "Hartigans_D", "Global_LID", "Opt_k")))
  
  # Identify the maximum Hartigan's D for highlighting
  max_dip <- plot_data |>
    filter(Metric == "Hartigans_D") |>
    filter(Value == max(Value, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    slice(1)
  
  # Identify the minimum LID for highlighting
  min_lid <- plot_data |>
    filter(Metric == "Global_LID") |>
    filter(Value == min(Value, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    slice(1)
  
  # Plot the 4-panel stability profile
  p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = Threshold, y = Value, color = Metric)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    geom_point(data = max_dip, fill = "gold", color = "red", size = 4, shape = 21, stroke = 1.2) +
    geom_point(data = min_lid, fill = "gold", color = "red", size = 4, shape = 21, stroke = 1.2) +
    facet_wrap(
      ~Metric, 
      scales = "free_y", 
      ncol = 1,
      labeller = as_labeller(c(
        N_Anomalies = "Number of Anomalies (N)",
        Hartigans_D = "Cluster Effect Size (Hartigan's Dip Statistic)", 
        Global_LID = "Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID)",
        Opt_k = "Optimal Clusters (k)"
      ))
    ) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(
      "N_Anomalies" = "#0072B2", 
      "Hartigans_D" = "#009E73", 
      "Global_LID" = "#CC79A7", 
      "Opt_k" = "#D55E00"
    )) +
    scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 10) +
    labs(
      title = plot_title,
      subtitle = plot_subtitle,
      x = "Anomaly Threshold",
      y = NULL
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), 
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      legend.position = "none",
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11)
    )
  
  return(p)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-naive-evaluate-stability
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Show Plot Call"
#| fig-cap: "Topological stability across anomaly thresholds using raw telemetry features. The volatility across all metrics indicates a lack of stable anomaly archetypes."
#| fig-height: 12
#| fig-width: 9
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Generate the Naive Plot
fig_naive <- plot_topological_stability(
  stability_curve_naive,
  plot_title = "Anomaly Threshold Diagnostics: Naive Configuration",
  plot_subtitle = "Mapping cluster plateaus (k), distance heterogeneity (D), and variable dependencies breaks (LID) to guide threshold exploration."
)

print(fig_naive)
```


@fig-naive-evaluate-stability shows candidate plateaus at $k = 4$, $k=3$ and $k=2$. We choose to ignore the plateau at $k=4$ because, while it spans the largest threshold interval, it still represents at least 200 points and its metrics $D$ and LID are not remarkable. The plateau at $k=2$ starts with the maximum $D$ value, indicating at least two very different types of distances in the Hamming matrix. The last small plateau at $k=3$ is also interesting because it indicates severe breakdown due to its small LID value.

Comparing values of diagnostic metrics $D$ and LID is in itself useful. One can also ask the following question: are those values "significantly" large or small? Answering such questions requires building null models of these two metrics. We start with metric $D$ by utilizing the helper function `simulate_empirical_null_dip`.

```{r}
#| label: naive-anomaly-thresholds
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Show Null Dip Computation"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(purrr)
library(dplyr)

# TB Modified: by = 5
n_sequence <- seq(20, 100, by = 20)

  dip_control_naive <- map_dfr(n_sequence, function(n) {
  res <- simulate_dip_control(engine, N = n, iterations = 200)
  res$Threshold <- get_threshold_at_N(engine, n)
  return(res)
})
```

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-null-dip
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Show ggplot function"

library(ggplot2)

# Define a reusable plotting wrapper for all null profiles
plot_baseline_profile <- function(results_df, line_color, plot_title, plot_subtitle, y_label) {
  ggplot(results_df, aes(x = Threshold)) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Q05, ymax = Q95), fill = line_color, alpha = 0.2) +
    geom_line(aes(y = Median), color = line_color, linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_point(aes(y = Median), color = line_color, size = 3) +
    scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 10) +
    labs(
      title = plot_title,
      subtitle = plot_subtitle,
      x = "Anomaly Threshold",
      y = y_label
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-naive-control-dip
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Show Plot Call"
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Simulated Control Bounds of Hartigan's Dip Statistic. The observed peak in the actual stacbility profile exceeds the 95% threshold, rejecting the possibility of the observed peak being due to using distances with Hartigan's test. Irregular sampling of the theshold is explained by sampling based on number of anomalies."

# Generate the Naive Dip Plot
fig_dip_null_naive <- plot_baseline_profile(
  dip_control_naive,
  line_color = "#D55E00", 
  plot_title = "Control Quantiles for Hartigan's D (Naive Configuration)",
  plot_subtitle = "Median and [5%, 95%] bounds estimated with Monte Carlo simulations.",
  y_label = "Hartigan's D"
)

print(fig_dip_null_naive)
```

@fig-naive-control-dip displays quantiles of a control distribution for $D$ obtained with the following simulation scheme at each value of $N$: we uniformly sample $N$ observations directly from the entire ingested time course, construct the Isolation Forest distance matrix for that subset, and compute Hartigan's $D$.

Repeated across Monte Carlo iterations, this establishes a baseline of expected distance heterogeneity. By sampling primarily from nominal operations, and not anomalies, the simulation preserves the multivariate dependencies of the dataset. This yields a conservative control to test whether the extracted anomalies exhibit greater distance heterogeneity than typical system variance.

In @fig-naive-evaluate-stability, we observed a maximum $D$ of approximately 0.06 near $T = 0.653$. In the control plot, the 95th percentile of the control distribution remains below 0.02 at this threshold and below 0.035 across the entire sweep. This gap holds at all values of $N$, confirming that the distance heterogeneity observed in the anomaly matrix is not an artifact of utilizing Hartigan's D with a distance matrix.

```{r}
#| label: naive-null-lid-profile-preparation
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Show Data Preparation (call to simulation helper)"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(purrr)
library(dplyr)

# Sweep the Monte Carlo simulation for the Naive Engine
# Reusing the n_sequence defined in the previous Dip chunk
lid_results_naive <- map_dfr(n_sequence, function(n) {
  res <- simulate_lid_control(engine, N = n, iterations = 200)
  res$Threshold <- get_threshold_at_N(engine, n)
  return(res)
})
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-lid-control
#| eval: false

#| code-summary: "Show Plot Call"

#| fig-width: 8

The observed drop in dimensionality with anomalies falls below the 5% lower bound, in agreement with the hypothesis of a structural break for detected anomalies. Irregular sampling of the theshold is explained by sampling based on number of anomalies."

message(sprintf("Simulating random healthy LID space across %d steps...", length(n_sequence)))

fig_lid_naive <- plot_baseline_profile(
  lid_results_naive,
  line_color = "#CC79A7", # Matches the exact purple/pink LID color from the stability panels
  plot_title = "Control Quantiles for Intrinsic Dimensionality (Naive Configuration)",
  plot_subtitle = "Median and [5%, 95%] bounds.",
  y_label = "Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID)"
)

print(fig_lid_naive)
```

@fig-lid-control shows the results obtained when applying the same control strategy to LID. This provides a baseline of expected local intrinsic dimensionality.

In @fig-naive-evaluate-stability, the last two plateaus ($k=2$ and $k=3$) are characterized by small values of LID: below the 95th percentile of values obtained with the control at same $N$. Therefore, it is likely that anomalies for $k=2$ and $k=3$ represent system breakdowns.

Next, we extract the cluster medoids (the centrally representative points of each cluster) utilizing the `extract_medoids` method. By setting the target k to NULL, the algorithm automatically calibrates and selects the optimal number of clusters by maximizing the global silhouette score.

Note that this method does not return an isolated data point. The engine utilizes the `temporal_window_hours` parameter defined in the YAML configuration. For each identified medoid, it returns the physical window surrounding the anomaly timestamp. Now, keep in mind that for this naive yaml configuration, features fed to the Isolation Forest are static ones: they have not been engineered to reflect change over time. Therefore, **the presented time windows are not explanatory of the anomalies**, only at best informative in terms of when they occur.

```{r}
#| label: naive-medoids-extraction
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Show Medoids Extraction"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)

# Target the threshold where Hartigan's D peaks
th_maxD_naive <- stability_curve_naive$Threshold[which.max(stability_curve_naive$Hartigans_D)]

# The optimal k will be automatically chosen
target_k <- NULL

# Extract anomalies, compute distances, calibrate the tree, and extract medoids in one step
engine <- extract_medoids(engine, threshold = th_maxD_naive, k = target_k)
```

<b id="medoids-ggplot-target" class="flash-target">Medoids Plotting Wrapper</b>
```{r}
#| label: medoids-ggplot-function
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Show Medoid Plot Function"

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)

# Define the medoid plotting wrapper
plot_medoid_trajectories <- function(medoid_engine, plot_title, plot_subtitle, label_style = "numeric", vars_to_plot = NULL) {
  
  raw_medoids <- get_medoids(medoid_engine)
  schema <- get_features(medoid_engine)
  
  # Allow targeting specific variables to prevent visual clutter
  if (is.null(vars_to_plot)) {
    plot_vars <- intersect(
      c(schema$context_variables, schema$target_variables), 
      colnames(raw_medoids)
    )
  } else {
    plot_vars <- intersect(vars_to_plot, colnames(raw_medoids))
  }
  
  format_var_name <- function(x) {
    str_to_title(str_replace_all(str_replace_all(x, "_15m", ""), "_", " "))
  }
  
  # Compute robust global bounds to anchor y-axes
  global_bounds <- medoid_engine@raw_time_course |>
    select(all_of(plot_vars)) |>
    pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") |>
    group_by(Variable) |>
    summarise(
      Min = quantile(Value, 0.01, na.rm = TRUE),
      Max = quantile(Value, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      Variable_Clean = factor(Variable, levels = plot_vars, labels = sapply(plot_vars, format_var_name))
    )
  
  blank_data <- bind_rows(
    global_bounds |> select(Variable_Clean, Value = Min),
    global_bounds |> select(Variable_Clean, Value = Max)
  )
  
  # Prepare plotting data with a Proximity weight for visual decay
  plot_data <- raw_medoids |>
    mutate(
      Relative_Time = as.numeric(difftime(timestamp, medoid_timestamp, units = "hours")),
      Archetype = if (label_style == "alpha") {
        paste("Archetype", LETTERS[as.numeric(str_extract(cluster, "\\d+"))])
      } else {
        str_replace(cluster, "Cluster", "Archetype")
      },
      Proximity = 1 - (abs(Relative_Time) / max(abs(Relative_Time), na.rm = TRUE))
    ) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = all_of(plot_vars),
      names_to = "Variable",
      values_to = "Value"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      Variable_Clean = factor(Variable, levels = plot_vars, labels = sapply(plot_vars, format_var_name))
    )
  
  p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = Relative_Time, y = Value, color = Variable_Clean)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_line(aes(alpha = Proximity, linewidth = Proximity)) +
    geom_point(
      data = function(x) filter(x, Relative_Time == 0), 
      shape = 21, 
      color = "black",          
      size = 3.5,               
      stroke = 0.8,             
      aes(fill = Variable_Clean)
    ) +
    geom_blank(data = blank_data, aes(x = 0, y = Value), inherit.aes = FALSE) + 
    facet_grid(Variable_Clean ~ Archetype, scales = "free_y") +
    scale_color_viridis_d(option = "turbo") + 
    scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "turbo") + 
    scale_alpha_continuous(range = c(0.2, 1), guide = "none") +
    scale_linewidth_continuous(range = c(0.4, 2), guide = "none") +
    labs(
      title = plot_title,
      subtitle = plot_subtitle,
      x = "Relative Time from Anomaly (Hours)",
      y = "Telemetry Value"
    ) +
    theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      legend.position = "none",
      strip.text.x = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
      strip.text.y = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, angle = 270), 
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80", linewidth = 0.5),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.spacing = unit(0, "pt"),
      panel.border = element_rect(color = "grey80", fill = NA, linewidth = 1.0)
    )
  
  return(p)
}
```


```{r}
#| label: fig-naive-medoids
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Show Medoids Plot Call"
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-cap: "Multivariate time-course trajectories for the two extracted HVAC fault archetypes at anomaly threshold $T=0.6534$. The physical window spans from two hours before to two hours after the detected anomaly timestamp (dashed vertical line)." 

# Visualization
fig_medoids_naive <- plot_medoid_trajectories(
  engine,
  plot_title = sprintf("Multivariate Trajectories of HVAC Faults (Naive Configuration, T=%.4f)", th_maxD_naive),
  plot_subtitle = "Archetypes extracted at the maximum Hartigan's D threshold."
)

print(fig_medoids_naive)
```


@fig-naive-medoids-plot shows that targeting the maximum distance heterogeneity with $D$ isolated two distinct physical faults. To properly interpret these faults under the naive configuration, we must look only at the anchor points at $t=0$, as these represent the only data the clustering algorithm evaluated.

- **Archetype 1** is characterized at $t=0$ by an actively running system in a warm, humid external environment (high T Outdoor and Rh Outdoor). The system is consuming Power and Energy, and the internal variables reflect an active cooling state with relatively moderate supply and return temperatures. The system might not be able to sufficiently cool the building at this anomaly timestamp.
- **Archetype 2** represents a different state. At $t=0$, the active Power reading sits exactly at zero in a cool, dry external environment. Despite these cooler ambient conditions, the internal temperatures (T Supply, T Return, T Saturation) are anomalously hot—significantly higher than those in Archetype 1. 


In conclusion, targeting the peak of Hartigan's $D$ maximized the distance between an actively powered, internally cool system operating in a warm environment, and an unpowered, internally hot system sitting in a cool environment.

We next illustrate the use of LID by extracting medoids at its lowest value.


```{r}
#| label: lid-medoids-extraction
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Show Medoids Extraction (Min LID)"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Target the threshold where Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID) is minimized
th_minLID_naive <- stability_curve_naive$Threshold[which.min(stability_curve_naive$Global_LID)]

# The optimal k will be automatically chosen (expected k=3 based on stability profile)
engine <- extract_medoids(engine, threshold = th_minLID_naive, k = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-lid-medoids-plot
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 12
#| fig-cap: "Multivariate time-course trajectories for the three extracted HVAC fault archetypes at the minimum LID threshold. The physical window spans from two hours before to two hours after the detected anomaly timestamp (dashed vertical line)."

# Call the plotting wrapper on the extracted medoids
fig_lid_medoids <- plot_medoid_trajectories(
  engine, 
  plot_title = "Multivariate Trajectories of HVAC Faults (Naive Configuration, Minimum LID)",
  plot_subtitle = "Archetypes extracted at the threshold of maximum variable coupling",
  label_style = "alpha"
)

print(fig_lid_medoids)
```


@fig-lid-medoids-plot illustrates the concept of clustering fragmentation which happens here at the minimum LID. Archetype B mirrors the previous Archetype 1. At $t=0$, the system is actively running at high power (Power $\approx 6$) with moderate internal temperatures.

Archetypes A and C are merely deviants of this same active state. While their instantaneous Power readings fluctuate at $t=0$ (dropping to $\approx 3$ in A, and $\approx 0$ in C), their internal thermodynamic states remain cool.

Also, the previous Archetype 2, characterized by an unpowered state and a spike in internal temperatures to $>25^\circ C$) is now missing. This shows that the large anomaly threshold required to minimize LID filtered out the fault represented by archetype 2. 

Now, @fig-naive-medoids-plot shows that, while it is not at its global minimum at T = 0.653 ($k=2$), LID is there at a visible local minimum. This is in agreement with the hypothesis of low LID being a good indicator of a fault.

Lastly, when fragmentation is suspected to be occuring in clustering, optional argument `k` can be utilized in method `extract_medoids` to perform a higher tree cut.

## Engineering Features for the Turin HVAC dataset

Utilizing the raw features of the Turin HVAC dataset yielded only two fault archetypes. Raw features are static in the sense that they do not include concept of temporal evolution of variables. To evaluate strategies of feature engineering that would better reflect dynamics of the system, a simple approach is to first look at a short continuous time course of the raw features.

```{r}
#| label: fig-data-exploration-all
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 12
#| fig-cap: "1-Week Time Course of All System Variables"

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)
library(isoRouting)

# 1. Load the bundled package data
data("hvac_features", package = "isoRouting")

# 2. Instantiate the engine and ingest data strictly through the API
engine_exploratory <- new("DiagnosticEngine", config_path = config_naive)
engine_exploratory <- ingest_time_course(engine_exploratory, data = hvac_features)

# 3. Retrieve the validated telemetry using the S4 getter
hvac_valid <- get_time_course(engine_exploratory)

# 4. Extract a 1-week subset for visualization
hvac_week <- hvac_valid |>
  filter(
    timestamp >= ymd("2019-11-01", tz = "UTC"), 
    timestamp < ymd("2019-11-08", tz = "UTC")
  ) 

# 5. Pivot and plot
hvac_plot_all <- hvac_week |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -timestamp, 
    names_to = "Variable", 
    values_to = "Value"
  )

ggplot(hvac_plot_all, aes(x = timestamp, y = Value, color = Variable)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~Variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Comprehensive 1-Week HVAC Telemetry",
    subtitle = "Turin Dataset: Nov 1 - Nov 7, 2019",
    x = "Time", 
    y = "Measurement"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

The most prominent characteristics in @fig-data-exploration-all are the step changes across variables like energy, power, and t_supply. These jumps reflect the causal, closed-loop control mechanics of the HVAC system: crossing a programmed threshold triggers a quick mechanical response.

These abrupt changes explain the geometric fragmentation previously observed in @fig-pairs-plot. Because the system rapidly changes between discrete operational states, the pairwise scatterplots manifest as isolated lines and dense clouds devoid of intermediate values. Since these sudden transitions drive the actual physical behavior of the unit, static values of sensor readings are insufficient. To isolate meaningful operational archetypes, we must engineer kinematic features—for instance short time derivatives—that encode these rates of change [@blazquez2021review; @cook2019anomaly].

We next present feature data analyses that justify the way we engineer them.

### Power and Energy

```{r}
#| label: fig-energy-power-mechanics
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Top: High-resolution marginal distributions of Energy and Power. Bottom: Transition matrices detailing the frequency of mechanical state changes (static continuous states are filtered out to highlight active transitions)."

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(patchwork)

# Define uniform factor levels to ensure heatmaps align correctly
state_levels <- c("Low", "Medium", "High")

# --- 1. Top Row: Histograms ---
p_hist_energy <- hvac_valid |>
  ggplot(aes(x = energy)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 150, fill = "#3b528b", color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(title = "Energy Distribution", x = "Energy", y = "Count") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

p_hist_power <- hvac_valid |>
  ggplot(aes(x = power)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 150, fill = "#21918c", color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(title = "Power Distribution", x = "Power", y = "Count") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

# --- 2. Data Prep: Transition Matrices ---
# Energy transitions
trans_energy <- hvac_valid |>
  select(timestamp, energy) |>
  mutate(
    state = case_when(
      energy >= 0 & energy < 5 ~ "Low",
      energy >= 5 & energy < 10 ~ "Medium",
      energy >= 10 ~ "High"
    ),
    state = factor(state, levels = state_levels),
    prev_state = lag(state)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(prev_state) & state != prev_state) |>
  count(prev_state, state, name = "Count")

# Power transitions
trans_power <- hvac_valid |>
  select(timestamp, power) |>
  mutate(
    state = case_when(
      power >= 0 & power < 2 ~ "Low",
      power >= 2 & power < 4 ~ "Medium",
      power >= 4 ~ "High"
    ),
    state = factor(state, levels = state_levels),
    prev_state = lag(state)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(prev_state) & state != prev_state) |>
  count(prev_state, state, name = "Count")

# --- 3. Bottom Row: Heatmaps ---
plot_heatmap <- function(data, title, fill_color) {
  ggplot(data, aes(x = prev_state, y = state, fill = Count)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_text(aes(label = Count), color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey80", high = fill_color) +
    scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
    scale_y_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    labs(title = title, x = "Previous State", y = "New State") +
    theme(
      legend.position = "none",
      panel.grid = element_blank(),
      axis.text = element_text(face = "bold")
    )
}

p_heat_energy <- plot_heatmap(trans_energy, "Energy Transitions", "#3b528b")
p_heat_power <- plot_heatmap(trans_power, "Power Transitions", "#21918c")

# --- 4. Combine with Patchwork ---
layout <- (p_hist_energy | p_hist_power) / (p_heat_energy | p_heat_power)
layout + plot_annotation(
  title = "Mechanical Dynamics: Distributions and Transitions",
  theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"))
)
```


@fig-energy-power-mechanics displays the distributions and state transitions for both variables. The top histograms show they operate in three discrete bands: Low, Medium, and High. The transition heatmaps reveal control loops that frequently bypass the intermediate state; for instance, power relies heavily on direct Low-to-High and High-to-Low jumps. A simple first derivative ($\Delta_{15m}$) would create numerical ambiguity—a Low-to-Medium jump and a Medium-to-High jump would yield similar gradients. To avoid this, severity of these jumps is encoded by using magnitude-weighted derivatives:
$$Value_t \times (Value_t - Value_{t-1})$$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-energy-power-mismatch
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Co-occurrence matrix of Energy and Power states. Off-diagonal tiles represent temporal desynchronization where instantaneous power and accumulated energy do not perfectly align."

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

state_levels <- c("Low", "Medium", "High")

# Prepare co-occurrence data
mismatch_data <- hvac_valid |>
  select(timestamp, energy, power) |>
  mutate(
    energy_state = factor(case_when(
      energy >= 0 & energy < 5 ~ "Low",
      energy >= 5 & energy < 10 ~ "Medium",
      energy >= 10 ~ "High"
    ), levels = state_levels),
    power_state = factor(case_when(
      power >= 0 & power < 2 ~ "Low",
      power >= 2 & power < 4 ~ "Medium",
      power >= 4 ~ "High"
    ), levels = state_levels)
  ) |>
  count(energy_state, power_state, name = "Count")

# Plot heatmap
ggplot(mismatch_data, aes(x = energy_state, y = power_state, fill = Count)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  # Dynamically change text color based on background darkness
  geom_text(aes(label = Count, color = Count > 1000), fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("black", "white")) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey95", high = "#e34a33", trans = "log10") + 
  scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
  scale_y_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title = "Energy vs. Power: State Co-occurrence",
    x = "Energy State (15-min Accumulated)",
    y = "Power State (Instantaneous)"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

@fig-energy-power-mismatch evaluates the assumption of colinearity between `energy` and `power` and shows hundreds of off-diagonal state mismatches. 

Therefore, in order to preserve mismatches as potential signs of an anomaly, we include both weighted derivatives of `energy` and `power` in our feature set:

`dw_power(t) = power(t)(power(t)-power(t-1))`<br>
`dw_energy(t) = energy(t)(energy(t)-energy(t-1))`

### Outdoor Environmental Variables

Unlike the abrupt mechanical step-changes of the HVAC equipment, environmental variables (`rh_outdoor` and `t_outdoor`) are expected to have slow, continuous variations over time. This is first quantified over the entire dataset by calculating the lag-1 autocorrelation coefficient (expected to be close to 1) and the standard deviation ratio, $\sigma_{\Delta} / \sigma_{\text{raw}}$, which compares the standard deviation of the 15-minute step changes to that of the raw variable (expected to be small compared to 1).

```{r}
#| label: smoothness-quantification
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true

library(dplyr)
library(stats)

hvac_valid |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  summarise(
    rh_autocorrelation = acf(rh_outdoor, lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE, na.action = na.pass)$acf[2],
    rh_sd_ratio = sd(rh_outdoor - lag(rh_outdoor), na.rm = TRUE) / sd(rh_outdoor, na.rm = TRUE),
    t_autocorrelation = acf(t_outdoor, lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE, na.action = na.pass)$acf[2],
    t_sd_ratio = sd(t_outdoor - lag(t_outdoor), na.rm = TRUE) / sd(t_outdoor, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  print()
```

The results confirm the continuous nature of these environmental features: both variables yield large autocorrelations (>0.99) and small standard deviation ratios (<0.14). 

```{r}
#| label: fig-outdoor-environment
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Distributions of raw values and 15-minute derivatives for outdoor relative humidity (left) and temperature (right). The narrow distributions of the derivatives highlight the slow, continuous nature of environmental shifts."

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Calculate derivatives
outdoor_features <- hvac_valid |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  select(timestamp, rh_outdoor, t_outdoor) |>
  mutate(
    rh_15m_diff = rh_outdoor - lag(rh_outdoor, n = 1),
    t_15m_diff = t_outdoor - lag(t_outdoor, n = 1)
  )

# --- 1. RH Plots (Left Column) ---
p_rh_raw <- ggplot(outdoor_features, aes(x = rh_outdoor)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100, fill = "#440154", color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(title = "Outdoor Humidity (Raw)", x = "Relative Humidity (%)", y = "Count")

p_rh_diff <- ggplot(outdoor_features, aes(x = rh_15m_diff)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100, fill = "#440154", color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(title = "15-Min Derivative (\u0394 15m)", x = "\u0394 RH (%)", y = "Count")

# --- 2. Temp Plots (Right Column) ---
p_t_raw <- ggplot(outdoor_features, aes(x = t_outdoor)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100, fill = "#c22b38", color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(title = "Outdoor Temperature (Raw)", x = "Temperature (\u00B0C)", y = "Count")

p_t_diff <- ggplot(outdoor_features, aes(x = t_15m_diff)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100, fill = "#c22b38", color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(title = "15-Min Derivative (\u0394 15m)", x = "\u0394 Temperature (\u00B0C)", y = "Count")

# --- 3. Combine with Patchwork ---
(p_rh_raw | p_t_raw) / (p_rh_diff | p_t_diff) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Environmental Dynamics: Outdoor Weather Sensors",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"))
  )
```

In agreement with the above results, the bottom panels of @fig-outdoor-environment show that the 15-minute first derivatives ($\Delta_{15m}$) for both temperature and humidity are tightly clustered around zero. This suggests that 15-minutes derivative might serve as a good feature for anomaly isolation: they allow the Isolation Forest to easily separate routine weather fluctuations from both sensor malfunctions (e.g., instantaneous $\pm50\%$ humidity dropouts) and severe meteorological events (e.g., sudden temperature plunges during storms).

`d_rh_outdoor(t) = rh_outdoor(t) - rh_outdoor(t-1)`<br>
`d_t_outdoor(t) = t_outdoor(t) - t_outdoor(t-1)`

### Indoor Return Temperature (t_return)

To explore the behavior of `t_return`, we first examine its raw distribution alongside its 15-minute and 1-hour temporal derivatives.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t-return-histograms
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Distributions of raw values and temporal derivatives for return temperature across the full dataset."

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

t_return_eda <- hvac_valid |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  select(timestamp, t_return) |>
  mutate(
    t_ret_15m_diff = t_return - lag(t_return, n = 1),
    t_ret_1h_diff = t_return - lag(t_return, n = 4)
  )

t_ret_long <- t_return_eda |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(t_return, t_ret_15m_diff, t_ret_1h_diff), 
    names_to = "metric", 
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    metric = factor(metric, 
                    levels = c("t_return", "t_ret_15m_diff", "t_ret_1h_diff"),
                    labels = c("Raw t_return (\u00B0C)", "15-Minute Derivative (\u0394 15m)", "1-Hour Derivative (\u0394 1h)"))
  )

ggplot(t_ret_long, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100, fill = "#c22b38", color = "black", linewidth = 0.1, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free", ncol = 1) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(x = "Value", y = "Frequency") +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

Unlike for outdoor environmental variables [@fig-outdoor-environment], the distribution of `t_return` is smooth and continuous, lacking coarse sensor discretization. In addition, the extended tails of the 1-hour derivative compared to the tight 15-minute derivative suggest that temperature changes compound over time. This hints at the presence of prolonged, continuous periods of active heating or cooling. To quantify the durations of these continuous phases, we apply Run Length Encoding (RLE). We classify 15-minute intervals with a derivative $> 0.05^\circ\text{C}$ as heating and $< -0.05^\circ\text{C}$ as cooling, calculating the total consecutive time spent in each state.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t-return-run-histograms
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Histogram of continuous heating and cooling durations, calculated using Run Length Encoding on the sign of the 15-minute derivative."

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

t_return_runs <- hvac_valid |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  mutate(
    t_ret_15m_diff = t_return - lag(t_return),
    diff_sign = case_when(
      t_ret_15m_diff > 0.05 ~ "Heating (Increasing)",
      t_ret_15m_diff < -0.05 ~ "Cooling (Decreasing)",
      TRUE ~ "Stable"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(diff_sign))

runs <- rle(t_return_runs$diff_sign)

run_df <- data.frame(
  state = runs$values,
  length_15m_intervals = runs$lengths
) |>
  filter(state != "Stable") |>
  mutate(duration_hours = length_15m_intervals * 0.25)

anno_df <- run_df |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarise(
    max_hrs = max(duration_hours),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(label = paste0("Max Duration:\n", max_hrs, " hours"))

ggplot(run_df, aes(x = duration_hours, fill = state)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 0, color = "black", alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~state, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  geom_text(
    data = anno_df,
    aes(x = 4.8, y = c(1000, 1000), label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    hjust = 1, vjust = 1, fontface = "bold", size = 4, color = "grey30"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Cooling (Decreasing)" = "#3b528b", "Heating (Increasing)" = "#c22b38")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 5, by = 0.5)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 5)) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(x = "Continuous Duration (Hours)", y = "Count of Occurrences") +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

@fig-t-return-run-histograms shows that continuous operational states can persist for nearly 6 hours.

In order for the Isolation Forests to recognize anomalous cooling and heating prolonged events, we explicitly incorporate them with the following tow engineered features.

- **Signed Duration (`t_ret_run_length`)**: An integer counter of how many consecutive intervals the system has been moving in the current direction (positive for heating, negative for cooling). This represents time spent in a continuous state.
- **Cumulative Displacement (t_ret_displacement)**: The total temperature change since the current continuous run began. This captures the intensity of the state, separating passive environmental drift (long duration, low displacement) from active mechanical forcing (long duration, high displacement).

These features are explicitly defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta \text{t\_return}_{15m}(t) &= \text{t\_return}(t) - \text{t\_return}(t-1) \\
\text{t\_ret\_run\_length}(t) &= k \times \text{direction} \\
\text{t\_ret\_displacement}(t) &= \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \Delta \text{t\_return}_{15m}(t-i)
\end{aligned}
$$
Where $k$ represents the number of consecutive 15-minute intervals in the current thermodynamic `direction` (-1 for cooling and +1 for heating).


### System Error, Thermal Effort, and Thermal Kinematics (`sp_return` & `t_supply`)

The variables `sp_return` (programmed setpoint) and `t_supply` (air exiting the mechanical unit) are final key controls of the HVAC loop. Their independent values do not directly convey the system's performance. For instance, a raw `t_supply` of $22^\circ\text{C}$ represents active heating if the room is $18^\circ\text{C}$, but represents active cooling if the room is $26^\circ\text{C}$.

To provide the Isolation Forest with a better geometric manifold of the system's physical state, we engineer these relationships into two gaps:

```{r}
#| label: fig-system-gaps
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Distributions of the Control Error (top) and Supply Delta (bottom). The Supply Delta captures the operational states: idling (the central spike at zero), active cooling (the left tail), active heating (the right mound), and extreme mechanical anomalies (the distant outliers)."

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

gaps_eda <- hvac_valid |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  select(timestamp, t_return, sp_return, t_supply) |>
  mutate(
    control_error = t_return - sp_return,
    supply_delta = t_supply - t_return
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(control_error) & !is.na(supply_delta))

gaps_long <- gaps_eda |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(control_error, supply_delta), 
    names_to = "metric", 
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    metric = factor(metric, 
                    levels = c("control_error", "supply_delta"),
                    labels = c("Control Error (t_return - sp_return)", 
                               "Supply Delta (t_supply - t_return)"))
  )

ggplot(gaps_long, aes(x = value, fill = metric)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 150, color = "black", alpha = 0.8, linewidth = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free", ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#3b528b", "#e35932")) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(x = "Temperature Difference (\u00B0C)", y = "Frequency") +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

- **Control Error (`control_error`)**: The difference between the actual room state and the programmed target. @fig-system-gaps (top) shows a broad, negatively skewed distribution. Large deviations in this feature allow the algorithm to isolate moments where the system is failing to keep up with the environmental load.
- **Thermal Effort (`supply_delta`)**: The $\Delta T$ across the room. @fig-system-gaps (bottom) cleanly separates the system's operational phases, isolating extreme mechanical effort (the distant outliers) from standard idling or active cycles.

Next, as we did with `t_return`, we explore the duration of active and cooling periods as now defined with `t_supply`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t-supply-run-histograms
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Histogram of continuous heating and cooling durations for supply air."

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

supply_runs <- hvac_valid |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  mutate(
    t_sup_15m_diff = t_supply - lag(t_supply),
    diff_sign = case_when(
      t_sup_15m_diff > 0.05 ~ "Heating (Increasing)",
      t_sup_15m_diff < -0.05 ~ "Cooling (Decreasing)",
      TRUE ~ "Stable"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(diff_sign))

runs <- rle(supply_runs$diff_sign)

run_df <- data.frame(
  state = runs$values,
  length_15m_intervals = runs$lengths
) |>
  filter(state != "Stable") |>
  mutate(duration_hours = length_15m_intervals * 0.25)

anno_df <- run_df |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarise(
    max_hrs = max(duration_hours),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(label = paste0("Max Duration:\n", max_hrs, " hours"))

ggplot(run_df, aes(x = duration_hours, fill = state)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 0, color = "black", alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~state, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  geom_text(
    data = anno_df,
    aes(x = Inf, y = Inf, label = label), 
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    hjust = 1.2, vjust = 1.5, fontface = "bold", size = 4, color = "grey30"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Cooling (Decreasing)" = "#3b528b", "Heating (Increasing)" = "#e35932")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, by = 0.5)) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(x = "Continuous Duration (Hours)", y = "Count of Occurrences") +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

(@fig-t-supply-run-histograms) shows that mechanical modulation phases can persist for up to 6 hours. To equip the Isolation Forest to detect these periods we perform a similar encoding to the one for `t_return`:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{control\_error}(t) &= \text{t\_return}(t) - \text{sp\_return}(t) \\
\text{supply\_delta}(t) &= \text{t\_supply}(t) - \text{t\_return}(t) \\
\Delta \text{t\_supply}_{15m}(t) &= \text{t\_supply}(t) - \text{t\_supply}(t-1) \\
\text{t\_sup\_run\_length}(t) &= j \times \text{direction} \\
\text{t\_sup\_displacement}(t) &= \sum_{i=0}^{j-1} \Delta \text{t\_supply}_{15m}(t-i)
\end{aligned}
$$
Where $j$ represents the number of consecutive 15-minute intervals moving in the same thermodynamic direction.

### Humidity and Condensation (`rh_return`, `rh_supply` & `t_saturation`)

Variables `rh_return`, `rh_supply`, and `t_saturation` monitor and control the moisture state of the HVAC system. Relative humidity and saturation temperature are inherently coupled to air temperature. 

To map these relationships, we engineer three differences:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{humidity\_delta}(t) &= \text{rh\_supply}(t) - \text{rh\_return}(t) \\ \text{supply\_margin}(t) &= \text{t\_supply}(t) - \text{t\_saturation}(t) \\ \text{return\_margin}(t) &= \text{t\_return}(t) - \text{t\_saturation}(t) \end{aligned}$$

```{r}
#| label: fig-moisture-gaps
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-cap: "Distributions of the engineered moisture gaps: Humidity Delta, Supply Margin, and Return Margin."

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

moisture_gaps_eda <- hvac_valid |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  select(timestamp, rh_return, rh_supply, t_supply, t_return, t_saturation) |>
  mutate(
    humidity_delta = rh_supply - rh_return,
    supply_margin = t_supply - t_saturation,
    return_margin = t_return - t_saturation
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(humidity_delta) & !is.na(supply_margin) & !is.na(return_margin))

moisture_long <- moisture_gaps_eda |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(humidity_delta, supply_margin, return_margin), 
    names_to = "metric", 
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    metric = factor(metric, 
                    levels = c("humidity_delta", "supply_margin", "return_margin"),
                    labels = c("Humidity Delta (rh_supply - rh_return) [%]", 
                               "Supply Margin (t_supply - t_saturation) [\u00B0C]",
                               "Return Margin (t_return - t_saturation) [\u00B0C]"))
  )

ggplot(moisture_long, aes(x = value, fill = metric)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 150, color = "black", alpha = 0.8, linewidth = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free", ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#0868ac", "#7bccc4", "#43a2ca")) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title = "EDA: Moisture Gaps and Saturation Margins",
    subtitle = "Distributions of engineered humidity and saturation relationships",
    x = "Difference",
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

As shown in @fig-moisture-gaps, the Humidity Delta maintains a broadly positive distribution, potentially reflecting an average trend towards active humidification.

The Supply Margin reveals multiple distinct operational clusters and notably includes a probability mass that drops into negative territory. 

The Return Margin also has both negative and positive components, but the distribution is less complex than that of the Supply Margin.

Providing the Isolation Forest with the above engineered features should allow it to map different moisture regimes to geometric manifolds then used for anomaly detection.

To determine if these moisture boundaries shift instantaneously or drift over time, we apply the same Run Length Encoding (RLE) methodology previously established for the temperature variables. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-moisture-gaps-rle
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Histograms of consecutive continuous ramping durations for the engineered moisture gaps."

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

# 1. Calculate the gaps and their 15m differences
moisture_rle_data <- hvac_valid |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  mutate(
    humidity_delta = rh_supply - rh_return,
    supply_margin = t_supply - t_saturation,
    return_margin = t_return - t_saturation
  ) |>
  mutate(
    hum_delta_diff = humidity_delta - lag(humidity_delta),
    sup_margin_diff = supply_margin - lag(supply_margin),
    ret_margin_diff = return_margin - lag(return_margin)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(hum_delta_diff) & !is.na(sup_margin_diff) & !is.na(ret_margin_diff))

# 2. Helper function to compute RLE for a given vector
compute_rle <- function(diff_vec, threshold, var_name) {
  directions <- case_when(
    diff_vec > threshold ~ "Increasing",
    diff_vec < -threshold ~ "Decreasing",
    TRUE ~ "Stable"
  )
  
  runs <- rle(directions)
  
  data.frame(
    variable = var_name,
    state = runs$values, length_15m = runs$lengths
  ) |>
    filter(state != "Stable") |>
    mutate(duration_hours = length_15m * 0.25)
}

# 3. Apply RLE to each gap
rle_hum <- compute_rle(moisture_rle_data$hum_delta_diff, threshold = 0.1, "Humidity Delta (%)")
rle_sup <- compute_rle(moisture_rle_data$sup_margin_diff, threshold = 0.05, "Supply Margin (\u00B0C)")
rle_ret <- compute_rle(moisture_rle_data$ret_margin_diff, threshold = 0.05, "Return Margin (\u00B0C)")

# Combine into one dataframe
all_runs <- bind_rows(rle_hum, rle_sup, rle_ret) |>
  mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = c("Humidity Delta (%)", "Supply Margin (\u00B0C)", "Return Margin (\u00B0C)")))

# 4. Compute maximum durations for text annotations
anno_df <- all_runs |>
  group_by(variable, state) |>
  summarise(
    max_hrs = max(duration_hours),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(label = paste0("Max:\n", max_hrs, " h"))

# 5. Plot the histograms on a grid
ggplot(all_runs, aes(x = duration_hours, fill = state)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 0, color = "black", alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_grid(variable ~ state, scales = "free_y") +
  geom_text(
    data = anno_df,
    aes(x = Inf, y = Inf, label = label), 
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    hjust = 1.2, vjust = 1.5, fontface = "bold", size = 3.5, color = "grey30"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Decreasing" = "#3b528b", "Increasing" = "#e35932")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 15, by = 1)) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title = "EDA: Continuous Ramping Durations for Moisture Gaps",
    subtitle = "Histograms of consecutive increasing/decreasing trajectories",
    x = "Continuous Duration (Hours)",
    y = "Count of Occurrences"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

As demonstrated in @fig-moisture-gaps-rle, while the majority of shifts resolve rapidly, the system also undergoes continuous moisture ramps stretching across several hours. Incorporating the temporal history of these margins is likely essential to describe the HVAC system functioning. This history is encoded as was done before with the temperature gaps: signed duration (run length) and cumulative displacement.

Let $x \in \{ \text{humidity\_delta, supply\_margin, return\_margin} \}$ represent a given moisture gap, and $j$ represent the number of consecutive 15-minute intervals moving in the same continuous direction. The complete set of engineered features mapping the system's moisture state is defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned} 
\text{humidity\_delta}(t) &= \text{rh\_supply}(t) - \text{rh\_return}(t) \\ 
\text{supply\_margin}(t) &= \text{t\_supply}(t) - \text{t\_saturation}(t) \\ 
\text{return\_margin}(t) &= \text{t\_return}(t) - \text{t\_saturation}(t) 
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned} 
\Delta x_{15m}(t) &= x(t) - x(t-1) \\ 
\text{run\_length}_x(t) &= j \times \text{direction} \\ 
\text{displacement}_x(t) &= \sum_{i=0}^{j-1} \Delta x_{15m}(t-i) 
\end{aligned}
$$

### Summary of Engineered Features


The feature engineering phase transforms the raw sensor logs into a 24-dimensional geometric manifold. The complete feature set is summarized in the table below using standard mathematical notation.

| Category | Engineered Feature | Mathematical Definition |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Power & Energy** | `dw_power(t)`<br>`dw_energy(t)` | $\text{power(t)} \times (\text{power}(t) - \text{power}(t-1))$<br>$\text{energy}(t) \times (\text{energy}(t) - \text{energy}(t-1))$ |
| **Outdoor Environment** | `d_rh_outdoor(t)`<br>`d_t_outdoor(t)` | $\text{rh\_outdoor}(t) - \text{rh\_outdoor}(t-1)$<br>$\text{t\_outdoor}(t) - \text{t\_outdoor}(t-1)$ |
| **Indoor Return Temp** | `d_t_return_15m(t)`<br>`t_ret_run_length(t)`<br>`t_ret_displacement(t)` | $\text{t\_return}(t) - \text{t\_return}(t-1)$<br>$k \times \text{direction}$<br>$\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \Delta \text{t\_return}_{15m}(t-i)$ |
| **System Error & Thermal Effort** | `control_error(t)`<br>`supply_delta(t)`<br>`d_t_supply_15m(t)`<br>`t_sup_run_length(t)`<br>`t_sup_displacement(t)` | $\text{t\_return}(t) - \text{sp\_return}(t)$<br>$\text{t\_supply}(t) - \text{t\_return}(t)$<br>$\text{t\_supply}(t) - \text{t\_supply}(t-1)$<br>$j \times \text{direction}$<br>$\sum_{i=0}^{j-1} \Delta \text{t\_supply}_{15m}(t-i)$ |
| **Moisture Gaps** | `humidity_delta(t)`<br>`supply_margin(t)`<br>`return_margin(t)` | $\text{rh\_supply}(t) - \text{rh\_return}(t)$<br>$\text{t\_supply}(t) - \text{t\_saturation}(t)$<br>$\text{t\_return}(t) - \text{t\_saturation}(t)$ |
| **Moisture Kinematics** <br>*(Where $x$ is each of the 3 moisture gaps)* | `d_x_15m(t)`<br>`run_length_x(t)`<br>`displacement_x(t)` | $x(t) - x(t-1)$<br>$m \times \text{direction}$<br>$\sum_{i=0}^{m-1} \Delta x_{15m}(t-i)$ |


## Archetype Extraction with Engineered Features

We now utilize the set of engineered features to extract fault archetypes.

### Engine Initialization

We initialize the engine, use the engineered-feature YAML configuration, and ingest the time course. To avoid scoring the massive 6-month summer gap as an anomaly, we again split the data into two parts (baseline_telemetry and stream_telemetry), utilizing split index `major_gap_idx` calculated during the [initial data validation step](#data-split-and-validation).

```{r}
#| label: engine-init-and-split
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Initialize Engine and Split Data"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)
library(isoRouting)
library(here)

# 1. Load the package data and configure the engine
data("hvac_features", package = "isoRouting")
config_engineered <- here("inst", "extdata", "engineered_features.yaml")
engine_engineered <- new("DiagnosticEngine", config_path = config_engineered)
engine_engineered <- ingest_time_course(engine_engineered, data = hvac_features)

# 2. Retrieve the validated telemetry mapped by the new YAML
hvac_valid_eng <- get_time_course(engine_engineered)

# 3. Bucket 1: Pre-Gap (~40% of data) for baseline archetype extraction
baseline_telemetry <- hvac_valid_eng |> 
  slice(1:major_gap_idx)

# 4. Bucket 2: Post-Gap (~60% of data) for predictive routing evaluation
stream_telemetry <- hvac_valid_eng |> 
  slice((major_gap_idx + 1):n())
```

### Isolation Forest Training and Score Distribution

With the continuous baseline (`baseline_telemetry`), we now fit the Isolation Forest model. The model dynamically pulls the ensemble size (500 trees) and sample size (256) from the engineered YAML configuration.

```{r}
#| label: fit-engineered-if
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Fit Isolation Forest"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)

# 1. Initialize a baseline-specific engine and ingest only the Winter 2019-2020 data
engine_baseline <- new("DiagnosticEngine", config_path = config_engineered)
engine_baseline <- ingest_time_course(engine_baseline, data = baseline_telemetry)

# 2. Fit the Isolation Forest and extract anomalies 
engine_baseline <- extract_anomalies(engine_baseline)

# 3. Retrieve the scores for the entire baseline dataset
baseline_scores <- stats::predict(engine_baseline@model, engine_baseline@feature_matrix)

baseline_scored <- baseline_telemetry |>
  mutate(anomaly_score = baseline_scores)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-engineered-if-dist
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Score Distribution"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of Isolation Forest anomaly scores with the engineered features."

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(baseline_scored, aes(x = anomaly_score)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100, fill = "#4c72b0", color = "black", alpha = 0.8, linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title = "Anomaly Score Distribution",
    subtitle = "Engineered features (Baseline: Winter 2019-2020)",
    x = "Anomaly Score",
    y = "Frequency"
  )
```

As seen in @fig-engineered-if-dist, the majority of standard telemetry is compressed below the anomaly score of 0.5. There are two distinct distribution bumps around 0.52 and 0.65. As was done previously with the naive configuration we next utilize method `evaluate_k_stability` to explore anomaly score thresholds. We do it here by varying the number $N$ of anomalies above the threshold.

### Threshold Diagnostics

We first utilize method `evaluate_k_stability` to retrieve the diagnostics profiles.

```{r}
#| label: engineered-evaluate-stability
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Run evaluate_k_stability"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Sweep based on size (N)
stability_curve_engineered <- evaluate_k_stability(
  engine_baseline, 
  max_N = 800, 
  min_N = 20, 
  nb_steps = 61, 
  max_k = 10
)
```

We then plot the profiles with the [previously defined wrapper](#stability-ggplot-target).

```{r}
#| label: fig-engineered-evaluate-stability
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Diagnostics Profile"
#| fig-cap: "Diagnositic scores across anomaly thresholds (800 < N < 20)."
#| fig-height: 12
#| fig-width: 9
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Generate the plot using the previously defined wrapper function
fig_engineered <- plot_topological_stability(
  stability_curve_engineered,
  plot_title = "Anomaly Threshold Diagnostics with Engineered Features",
  plot_subtitle = "Optimal cluster number (k), distance heterogeneity (D), and variable dependencies breaks (LID)."
)

print(fig_engineered)
```

@fig-engineered-evaluate-stability shows that distance heterogeneity between anomalies (D) is maximum between thresholds 0.59 and 0.61. In this interval, uncoupling between variables (LID) remains high, before following an overall decreasing trend. Therefore, we choose to explore the anomalies at threshold T = 0.6.

### Medoids Extraction

We now extract the medoids (representatives of clustered anomalies) at T = 0.6.

```{r}
#| label: extract-engineered-medoids
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Extract Archetypes at T = 0.6"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# 1. Isolate the top anomalies right after Hartigan's D peak
engine_baseline <- extract_medoids(engine_baseline, threshold = 0.6)

# 2. Retrieve the extracted physical archetypes (medoids)
medoids_df <- get_medoids(engine_baseline)

# 3. Print the mathematically calibrated k-value
cat("Mathematically Calibrated k at threshold = 0.6:", engine_baseline@optimal_k, "\n")
```

As shown above, the optimal number of clusters (maximum global silhouette score) is k = 4 at T = 0.6. 

We next display the time course of the extracted medoids utilizing the [previously defined wrapper](#medoids-ggplot-target) and visualizing only the `context_variables` defined in the YAML configuration.

```{r}
#| label: fig-engineered-comprehensive-medoids
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Archetype Trajectories"
#| fig-cap: "Time-course of the extracted 4 anomaly archetypes at T = 0.6."
#| fig-height: 14
#| fig-width: 10
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Retrieve the 10 context variables defined in the YAML
schema <- get_features(engine_baseline)
context_vars <- schema$context_variables

# Generate the plot
fig_medoids_comprehensive <- plot_medoid_trajectories(
  engine_baseline,
  plot_title = "Trajectories of the Four Archetypes at T = 0.6",
  plot_subtitle = "Trajectories of the context variables.",
  label_style = "numeric",
  vars_to_plot = context_vars
)

print(fig_medoids_comprehensive)
```

@fig-engineered-comprehensive-medoids is described as follows.

- **Archetype 1:** Characterized by a dip in supply temperature and a simultaneous spike in supply relative humidity at $t=0$. Return variables, outdoor variables, and the return setpoint remain stable. Power and energy show no deviation. This profile indicates a brief, unpowered humidity disturbance, which disrupts the supply air moisture without engaging the unit's power.   
- **Archetype 2:** Likely represents a commanded system startup. At $t=0$, both power and energy exhibit a large, sustained step-up from near zero. This is instantly coupled with a rise in both supply and return temperatures. Consequently, the supply and return relative humidity drop, reflecting heating air without adding moisture. The return setpoint and outdoor variables remain constant.   
- **Archetype 3:** Defines a thermal anomaly. The supply temperature undergoes a large, upward spike at $t=0$ and remains elevated. This temperature surge drives down the supply relative humidity. However, unlike Archetype 2, power and energy remain flat and near zero. This decoupling of thermal output from electrical input suggests an external mechanical failure.   
- **Archetype 4:** Represents a hard system shutdown or loss of power. The electrical power and energy drop instantaneously to zero. As a result, the supply and return temperatures begin a continuous downward decay. Inversely, the supply and return relative humidity climb steadily. The setpoint and outdoor variables remain flat throughout the decay.

In order to facilitate interpretation of the archetypes, `isoRouting` implements Leave One Covariate Out (LOCO) ablation tests in method `ablate_features`. Namely, anomaly scores of the extracted medoids are recomputed after setting one of the `target_variables` to its median value over the entire dataset. This is done for each target variable, and they are then sorted for their contribution to the archetype anomaly score.

```{r}
#| label: ablation-tests
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Ablation Tests"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

ablation_results <- ablate_features(engine_baseline)
```

```{r}
#| label: ablation-ggplot-function
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Show Ablation Plot Function"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# Reusable ablation plotting wrapper
plot_ablation_importance <- function(ablation_df, top_n = 5, plot_title, plot_subtitle) {
  
  # Filter to Top N drivers per cluster and retain raw variable names
  plot_data <- ablation_df |>
    group_by(cluster) |>
    slice_head(n = top_n) |>
    ungroup() |>
    mutate(
      # Create a unique factor for faceted reordering using the raw variable name
      var_ordered = factor(paste(cluster, variable, sep = "__"))
    ) |>
    # Reorder based on the magnitude of the score drop
    mutate(var_ordered = reorder(var_ordered, score_drop))
  
  # Generate the plot
  p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = score_drop, y = var_ordered, fill = cluster)) +
    geom_col(color = "black", linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.8) +
    facet_wrap(~cluster, scales = "free_y") +
    # Strip the cluster prefix to display just the raw variable name
    scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) gsub(".*__", "", x)) +
    scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "turbo") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
    labs(
      title = plot_title,
      subtitle = plot_subtitle,
      x = "Anomaly Score Drop (Contribution Magnitude)",
      y = "Engineered Feature (Raw)"
    ) +
    theme(
      legend.position = "none",
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80"),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
    )
  
  return(p)
}
```

```{r}
# 2. Generate the plot using the wrapper

  ablation_results,

)
```
